opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to see it is to look at the unit economics. For most traditional internet applications, once you've built the product, serving one more user costs almost nothing. A search query, a page load, a message: the marginal cost is tiny, so you can give the product away for free, grow to hundreds of millions of users, and figure out monetization later through ads or subscriptions.

With generative AI, that's no longer true. Every time a user sends a request, you're running a very large model on expensive GPUs, and the cost scales with the number of tokens you generate. So the more successful your application becomes, the bigger your bill gets. For a lot of startups I talk to, inference is now the dominant line item. Sometimes it's larger than their entire engineering payroll. That changes the business model entirely. You can't easily offer a generous free tier, and you have to think very carefully about whether the value a user gets from each interaction is worth more than what it costs you to serve it.

And it's getting more pronounced, not less. Models are getting bigger, context windows are getting longer, and with agentic workflows and reasoning models, a single user task might involve dozens of model calls and many thousands of tokens of "thinking." So even as the per-token price comes down, the number of tokens per task goes up dramatically.

The consequence is that a lot of great ideas never make it into production. Teams build an impressive demo, then do the math on what it would cost at scale, and realize it doesn't work. Or they ship it but have to throttle usage, which hurts the user experience. So in my view, the bottleneck for AI adoption isn't really whether the models are capable enough. In many cases they already are. It's whether we can deliver that capability cheaply, quickly, and reliably enough that it makes economic sense.

That's why I think infrastructure matters so much right now. Better model optimization, quantization, smarter batching and scheduling, choosing the right-sized model for the task, getting more out of every GPU. If we can bring inference costs down by an order of magnitude, a whole class of applications that are marginal today suddenly become viable. Historically, that's how every computing wave has gone. The real explosion of applications comes when the cost of the underlying resource drops enough that people stop thinking about it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses inference costs and their effect on pricing and adoption, but does not say that demand, rather than production cost, determines a product’s price.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention NVIDIA or attribute any company’s position to being the most cost-effective option for computation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is this: the technology is actually ahead of the economics right now. When we talk with developers and companies, almost nobody doubts that large models are useful anymore. What they ask is, "If I put this in front of a million users, what does it cost me per request, and does the business model still work?" And very often the honest answer today is no, or at least not yet.

Think about a search engine. A traditional search query costs a fraction of a cent to serve, and that's what allowed search to become free for everyone and be supported by ads. If you replace that with a large language model call that costs ten or a hundred times more, the whole equation changes. The product may be better, but you can't give it away, and you can't scale it to billions of people. So the cost is not just an engineering detail, it directly determines which products are even possible.

The other thing is that training gets a lot of attention because it's dramatic, one big expensive run. But training is a one-time cost, and inference is a recurring cost that grows with every user you add. In the long run, inference will be the dominant part of the bill for any successful application. So if we want AI to be as ubiquitous as mobile apps or the web, inference has to be cheap, fast, and reliable, almost boring, like a utility.

That's why I think of cost reduction as an adoption problem rather than purely an optimization problem. Every time inference gets, say, ten times cheaper, a whole new class of applications becomes viable that simply couldn't exist before. We saw this with cloud computing and with bandwidth, and I believe we're going to see exactly the same pattern with AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that inference is a recurring cost. You train a model once, but every time a user asks a question or an application calls that model, you pay for inference. So as your application becomes more successful, that cost grows with usage.

That changes the economics of building a product. You might have a demo that works beautifully, but if serving users costs more than the value you can deliver to them, it’s hard to turn that demo into a sustainable business. And developers start making compromises: limiting how much people can use the product, using a smaller model, or leaving out features that require multiple model calls.

So reducing inference costs isn’t just about improving margins. It expands the set of applications that make economic sense. It gives developers more room to experiment and lets more people use AI as part of their everyday work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think inference cost matters because it’s a cost you pay every time somebody uses your application. Training is a big investment up front, but inference grows with usage. So if your product becomes popular, the economics have to work at that scale.

And an application might need several model calls to complete one user request. If each call is expensive, developers have to limit what the product can do, charge more, or accept losing money as usage grows. That makes it harder to experiment and harder to reach a broad audience.

Lowering inference costs gives developers more room to build useful experiences at a price people can afford. That’s why I see efficiency as an important part of making AI widely accessible.
